title: Radical prostatectomy
what: The surgeon removes the whole prostate gland. The surgery is done under general anesthesia, often through small cuts.
why: Usually for prostate cancer, when the tumor has not spread beyond the gland.
duration: surgery usually takes 2 to 4 hours; the hospital stay is usually a few days; the catheter usually stays 1 to 2 weeks
tell_doctor: All your medicines, especially blood thinners. The doctor will tell you what to stop and when
Allergies, including to medicines and iodine
Heart, lung, or kidney disease, or diabetes
If you or your relatives had problems with anesthesia
How your peeing and erections are now

prepare.title: Tests
prepare.text: Blood tests, an ECG, and sometimes a checkup with a general doctor. The clinic will give you a list.

prepare.title: Anesthesiologist
prepare.text: Before surgery, the anesthesiologist will talk with you. Tell them about your health and medicines.

prepare.title: Food
prepare.text: Usually no food from the evening before and no drinks for a few hours before. The clinic will tell you the exact time.

prepare.title: Bowel
prepare.text: Sometimes you are asked to empty your bowel the day before. The clinic will give you instructions.

bring: Things for a few days in the hospital
steps: On the day of surgery, you change, and an IV line is placed in your vein
In the operating room, you get anesthesia and fall asleep
The surgeon removes the prostate through small cuts or one larger cut
The urethra is joined to the bladder
A catheter is placed in the bladder
You wake up in the recovery room
feel: After anesthesia, you may feel sleepy and sometimes sick
Pain at the cuts. You will get pain medicine
The catheter is bothersome, but you get used to it
after: The catheter is usually removed after 1 to 2 weeks. The doctor will tell you
Leaking urine after the catheter comes out is common and gets less over time
Pelvic floor exercises help. The doctor will explain them
No heavy lifting for a few weeks
Tissue test results are given at your follow-up visit
red_flags: A fever over 38°C or severe belly pain
Urine does not flow through the catheter: call the clinic or emergency services
Pain and swelling in a leg, or shortness of breath: call emergency services

faq.a: Right after the catheter comes out, leaking is common. For most men, it gets less over time.
It depends on the surgery and how things were before. Talk with your surgeon ahead of time. They will tell you what is realistic in your case.

reminders.text: Surgery tomorrow. Pack your things, documents, and list of medicines. Eat and drink only until the time the clinic gave you.
